newsitem.title: USA: Bell Atlantic, NYNEX reach merger accord with FCC.
newsitem.headline: Bell Atlantic, NYNEX reach merger accord with FCC.

text.p: Bell Atlantic Corp and NYNEX Corp Saturday said they had agreed to a set of commitments with federal regulators to open their local markets to rivals that could speed approval of their merger.

The two companies are seeking authorisation of a planned $23.7 billion merger from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission -- the final approval necessary to close the deal. They made the commitments in letter to the FCC.
In response, Chairman Reed Hundt and two of the FCC's four other commissioners said the merger should be approved.

The merger would create the nation's largest local phone company with a footprint reaching from Maine to Virginia and capable of offering residential and business customers a range of local, wireless and Internet access services.

The commitments cover a variety of issues that competitors seeking to enter local markets -- including long- distance carriers AT&T Corp and MCI Communications Corp -- complain make it unwieldy or too costly to do so now.

Tom Tauke, NYNEX's regulatory affairs chief, said in a conference call on Saturday detailing the companies' plans that, "all of these items are consistent with our general efforts to lower the barriers to competition."

In a statement, Hundt said: "The merger conditions proposed today by Bell Atlantic and NYNEX would bring enforceable, pro-competitive, market-opening terms to the whole Bell Atlantic/NYNEX region in a way that offsets the loss of Bell Atlantic as a potential competitor to NYNEX."
Critics have said the merger would reduce local phone competition by allowing Bell Atlantic and NYNEX, potential competitors in the other's adjacent service regions, to merge.
But regulators have signalled their willingness to see the merger go through if the companies consent to measures designed to open their local phone markets to wider competition.

"Based on these conditions, I personally believe we can and should approve the merger in the public interest," Hundt said. He was joined by FCC commissioners Susan Ness and James Quello in calling for the merger to be approved.

Besides opening Bell Atlantic/NYNEX local markets to competition, company officials said the new commitments could position a merged Bell Atlantic for early entry into the long distance business for customers in its service region.
"We think they are consistent with our efforts to enter the long-distance business," Taube said.

NYNEX has said it plans to offer long-distance services in New York state in the fourth quarter of 1997, while Bell Atlantic plans to offer long distance in one of its states, possibly Pennsylvania or West Virginia.

After weeks of questioning about merger details by FCC staff, the deal was arrived at during two days of talks between company lawyers and FCC staff members culminating Friday night in an agreement to make the commitments.

Merger approval could come within two weeks, officials at Bell Atlantic and NYNEX said, assuming FCC staff issue an order approving the merger and FCC commissioners review and vote to approve the order giving the merger the go-ahead.
Bell Atlantic and NYNEX said they had agreed to conditions in five categories:

-- Performance standards will be negotiated with competitors wishing to connect to the Bell Atlantic/NYNEX network, with enforcement mechanisms to ensure standards are met and state-level arbitration if the parties fail to agree.
-- Reporting requirements that call for the companies to diclose to the FCC statistics on service and network quality.

-- Uniform methods for connecting competitors to the Bell Atlantic/NYNEX operational support system that would make it easier for rivals to handle ordering, installation, billing and other customer service requirements without delays.
-- Flexible payment plans to avoid saddling new local service competitors, especially smaller players, with large up-front payments to Bell Atlantic/NYNEX for network access.

-- Forward-looking pricing would be enshrined as the method by which Bell Atlantic/NYNEX would seek pricing changes from regulators, instead of attempting to recover costs for previously installed equipment.
Currently, the companies report key operating statistics to state regulators, but give little information to the FCC.

Speaking to reporters, Tauke said it was difficult to estimate the costs of delivering on the commitments, but that no charges to earnings were expected to result. The agreements contain a four-year sunset provision, he said.
In an interview with Reuters, FCC Commissioner Ness said that, "this deal provides us with an enforcement role." Most local service oversight is handled by state regulators now.

Industry analyst Jeffrey Kagan of Kagan Telecom Associaties in Atlanta, said it remains to be seen how far the committments Bell Atlantic and NYNEX announced would go in breaking the stalemate that had slowed local competition.
"They are not commiting to peformance standards, They are just commiting to negotiate performance standards," he said.
